evidence.title: Automated Diabetic Retinopathy Screening in Out-patient Diabetes Care - Comparison of Two Artificial Intelligence Algorithms: RetCAD and OphtAI
evidence.outcome: Local outpatient clinic performance of DR AI compared with ophthalmologist reference and prior study conditions
evidence.effect: RetCAD's local sensitivity (90%) and specificity (100%) were consistent with study conditions; OphtAI was less sensitive (70%), missing patients with moderate DR.
evidence.quote: The AI-based algorithm OphtAI, on the other hand, detected fewer patients with moderate DR, which was reflected in lower sensitivity.

evidence.title: Computer-Aided Detection Colonoscopy for Surveillance in IBD Patients: Insights from a Single-Center Experience
evidence.outcome: Adenoma detection rate in local IBD population after CADe introduction
evidence.effect: Collective ADR 5.2% pre-CADe vs 3.8% after CADe (P = .315); nonsignificant decline, no improvement in neoplasm detection in IBD patients.
evidence.quote: In a real-world, single-center experience, the introduction of CADe did not improve neoplasms detection in patients with IBD and was associated with a nonsignificant decline in ADR.

evidence.title: Real-World Evaluation of AI-Driven Diabetic Retinopathy Screening in Public Health Settings: Validation and Implementation Study
evidence.outcome: Local diagnostic performance of commercial DR algorithms versus human reference standard
evidence.effect: Wide variability; AI-3 sensitivity 68.3% below FDA 85% benchmark; one algorithm detected DR in 89.2% of eyes vs 27.48% by reference standard.
evidence.quote: The three AI algorithms demonstrated variable diagnostic performance, with sensitivity (60%-80%) and specificity (14%-96%).

evidence.title: AI-enabled POCUS for breast cancer risk stratification in a resource-limited tertiary clinic
evidence.outcome: Local diagnostic accuracy of AI POCUS versus histopathology in local patients
evidence.effect: Sensitivity 67.2%, specificity 79.4%, PPV 70.3% at 51% threshold; AUC 0.76, moderate discriminatory performance
evidence.quote: Among 159 participants, Breast AI achieved a sensitivity of 67.2%, specificity of 79.4% and PPV of 70.3% at a 51% threshold.

evidence.title: A Machine Learning-Based Clinical Decision Support System to Improve End-of-Life Care
evidence.outcome: Model discrimination in local deployment versus model development performance
evidence.effect: Model discrimination was substantially worse than in model development; model was withdrawn from production after 16 months. Implementation did not improve palliative care consults or DNAR orders.
evidence.quote: The model discrimination was substantially worse than that observed in model development, and after 16 months, it was withdrawn from production.

evidence.title: Real-World Integration of an Automated Tool for Intracranial Hemorrhage Detection in an Unselected Cohort of Emergency Department Patients-An External Validation Study
evidence.outcome: Local performance of RAPID ICH versus prior studies on consecutive ED NCCTs
evidence.effect: Sensitivity 87.3%, specificity 74%, PPV 21.3%, NPV 98.6%; 8 false negatives and 203 false positives among 844 NCCTs. Lower than prior RAPID ICH studies.
evidence.quote: RAPID ICH's sensitivity and specificity were lower than in prior studies performed using RAPID ICH, and there was a high number of false-positive RAPID ICH identifications, limiting the generalizability of the assessed version of this DL tool.

evidence.title: Diagnostic performance of real-time characterization in artificial intelligence-assisted colonoscopy
evidence.outcome: Local diagnostic accuracy of CADx for diminutive rectosigmoid polyps against histopathology
evidence.effect: Sensitivity 93% (95% CI 87%-97%), specificity 33% (95% CI 22%-46%), PPV 70%, NPV 74%, accuracy 71%; specificity significantly lower than prior studies.
evidence.quote: The CADx-system demonstrated high sensitivity, but significantly lower specificity compared with prior studies, driven by a high false-positive rate.

evidence.title: Development and Prospective Validation of a Machine Learning Tool for Predicting Multidrug-resistant Organism Infections in an Indian Critical Care Unit
evidence.venue: Indian journal of critical care medicine : peer-reviewed, official publication of Indian Society of Critical Care Medicine
evidence.outcome: Gap between training and test accuracy of random forest model
evidence.effect: Training accuracy 96.0% versus test-set accuracy 75.3%, indicating overfitting.
evidence.quote: While the performance discrepancy between training and testing indicates overfitting, the high specificity and sensitivity observed in the prospective pilot phase support its potential as a bedside aid for early antimicrobial stewardship (AMS).
evidence.sample_unit: patients (prospective validation cohort; 323 in retrospective development)

evidence.title: Mobile AI-Assisted Oral Lesion Triage for Community Oral Cancer Screening: Prospective Field Evaluation Study
evidence.outcome: Field performance of AI red triage for high-risk lesions versus expert reference in low-prevalence setting
evidence.quote: For high-risk lesion identification, sensitivity was 75.0% (95% CI 50.5%-89.8%) and positive predictive value was 17.6% (95% CI 10.4%-28.4%); specificity, negative predictive value, and accuracy were 98.6%, 99.9%, and 98.5%, respectively.

evidence.title: Implementation of an artificial intelligence-based system for mammography in the compulsory medical insurance program: results of a 3-year study
evidence.venue: Quantitative imaging in medicine and surgery
evidence.outcome: Local performance vs developer-declared metrics
evidence.effect: CalT1 specificity 0.70 vs declared 0.88 (−20.45%); accuracy 0.77 vs 0.85 (−9.41%); CalT2 accuracy −12.94%.
evidence.quote: Subsequent calibration tests revealed initially subthreshold performance (AUC 0.83, accuracy 0.77, sensitivity 0.84, specificity 0.70), consistent with similar studies where early AI assessments uncover refinement needs ( 52 , 53 ).

evidence.title: Multi-Site Real-World Performance of Commercial AI for Pulmonary and Incidental Pulmonary Embolism Detection
evidence.outcome: Sensitivity and specificity of FDA-cleared PE AI on local historical data versus clearance benchmarks
evidence.effect: PE model 86.8% sensitivity, 99.1% specificity; iPE model 73.5% sensitivity, 99.8% specificity. Sensitivity was lower than FDA-clearance benchmarks while specificity exceeded them.
evidence.quote: Both models demonstrated lower sensitivity than FDA-clearance benchmarks while exceeding cleared specificity, with diminishing performance for peripheral and non-acute emboli mirroring known human reader limitations and underscoring the need for standardized post-market surveillance of AI-enabled medical devices.
evidence.sample_unit: CT examinations (30,678 CTPA and 37,191 routine contrast-enhanced CTs)

evidence.title: Clinical Validation of AI/ML Based Model for Down Syndrome Detection Through Graphical Analysis of Facial Dysmorphic Features
evidence.outcome: Local performance of the model on Indian children versus 98%+ controlled-experiment accuracy
evidence.effect: Sensitivity 100%, specificity 80%, average precision 96.6%, precision 86.67%, recall 92.86% at threshold 0.5, versus 98%+ accuracy in the controlled experiment.
evidence.quote: The CloudML model trained with 104 images initially achieved: Sensitivity - 100%, specificity - 80%, Average Precision - 96.6%, precision - 86.67%, and Recall - 92.86% (Precision and Recall are calculated at a confidence threshold of 0.5)

evidence.title: Screening Performance and Implementation Determinants of an AI-Assisted Visual Inspection application for Cervical Cancer Screening in Rwanda
evidence.outcome: AI-VIA sensitivity and specificity versus expert consensus on local patients, compared with nurse assessment
evidence.effect: AI sensitivity 33.3% (95% CI 18.0–51.8), specificity 92.2% (87.8–95.4); nurse sensitivity 51.5%, specificity 98.2%.
evidence.quote: Relative to expert consensus, nurse assessment demonstrated higher screening performance than the AI algorithm, with sensitivity 51.5% (95% CI 33.5–69.2) and specificity 98.2% (95% CI 95.4–99.5) versus sensitivity 33.3% (95% CI 18.0–51.8) and specificity 92.2% (95% CI 87.8–95.4).

evidence.title: Unverified Vendor Claims and Preventable Harms: A Mixed-Methods Longitudinal Independent Audit of Health AI System Performance in Nigeria
evidence.outcome: Local real-world performance versus developer/vendor evidence
evidence.effect: Gaps ranged from 17 to 35 percentage points and were statistically significant for all systems; estimated 1,247 undetected TB cases (186 preventable deaths) and 342 misclassified high-risk pregnancies annually.
evidence.quote: Gaps ranged from 17 to 35 percentage points and were statistically significant for all systems.

evidence.title: Community Learning Ledgers for Cancer Navigation in Small Island Developing States
evidence.outcome: performance in local context
evidence.effect: Ungoverned AI systems failed local cancer navigation, with the best scoring 68% and a physician platform scoring 7%.
evidence.quote: Every ungoverned AI system we tested failed Caribbean cancer navigation.
evidence.sample_unit: patient screening queries (plus 207 community sessions descriptively classified)
evidence.country: Caribbean (ten jurisdictions, led by Trinidad and Tobago)

evidence.title: Real-World Performance of Large Vessel Occlusion Artificial Intelligence-Based Computer-Aided Triage and Notification Algorithms-What the Stroke Team Needs to Know
evidence.venue: Journal of the American College of Radiology : JACR
evidence.outcome: Real-world sensitivity versus manufacturer-reported sensitivity for LVO detection at two stroke centers
evidence.effect: Hospital A: manufacturer sensitivity 97%; real-world 85.3% (ICA/M1), 68.5% with M2, 59.9% all proximal segments. Hospital B: manufacturer 87.8%; real-world 76.4% with M2, 59.4% all segments.
evidence.quote: Sensitivity decreased to 68.5% when M2 segments were included and to 59.9% when all proximal vessel segments were included.
evidence.sample_unit: code stroke CT angiography examinations (704 at hospital A, 642 at hospital B)

evidence.title: Implementation of artificial intelligence for the detection of cutaneous melanoma within a primary care setting: prevalence and types of skin cancer in outdoor enthusiasts
evidence.outcome: AI melanoma detection performance on local clinical population against histopathology
evidence.effect: Sensitivity 53.33%, specificity 54.44%, accuracy 54.17% in this clinical population, lower than expected from prior published performance.
evidence.quote: The performance of the AI from this clinical population was found to have a sensitivity of 53.33%, specificity of 54.44% and accuracy of 54.17%.
evidence.sample_unit: suspicious pigmented lesions (histopathology-confirmed MM n=15, benign n=33) from 423 participants

evidence.title: The Vienna Prediction Model for identifying patients at low risk of recurrent venous thromboembolism: a prospective cohort study
evidence.outcome: Underestimation of recurrent VTE risk in the prospective local cohort
evidence.effect: At 2 years, the observed/expected event ratio was 52/32 = 1.6 (95% CI 1.2–2.0), indicating underestimation of recurrence probabilities.
evidence.quote: The ratio of observed and expected events (O/E ratio), equal to 52/32 = 1.6 (95% CI 1.2–2.0), indicated general underestimation of recurrence probabilities.

evidence.title: Validation and three years of clinical experience in using an artificial intelligence algorithm as a second read system for prostate cancer diagnosis-real-world experience
evidence.outcome: Local validation accuracy on Puerto Rican cohort vs original developer populations
evidence.effect: Cancer detection AUC 0.994 (95% CI 0.988-0.997), sensitivity 96.6%, specificity 96.7%, NPV 99.2%; Gleason GG1 vs GG2+ AUC 0.901, similar to original populations.
evidence.quote: Results show a similar high diagnostic accuracy for cancer in this Puerto Rican population as in the original populations vs benign with an AUC of 0.994 (95% CI: 0.988–0.997).
evidence.sample_unit: cases (122,441 slides) in 3-year deployment; validation 101 cases/1279 slides

evidence.title: Single-center outcomes of artificial intelligence in management of pulmonary embolism and pulmonary embolism response team activation
evidence.venue: Journal of investigative medicine : the official publication of the American Federation for Clinical Research
evidence.outcome: False positive rate of AI PE detection on local CTPA versus radiologist report
evidence.effect: 57 of 200 exams (28.5%) correctly positive; 143 (71.5%) incorrectly positive; false positive rate 71.5% versus prior validation of 91% sensitivity, 100% specificity.
evidence.quote: The false positive rate of our AI algorithm was 71.5%, higher than what was reported in the AI's prior clinical validity study (91% sensitivity, 100% specificity).
evidence.sample_unit: CTPA exams flagged by AI as suspected PE

evidence.title: Performance of Automated Algorithm in Large and Medium Vessel Occlusion Detection: A Real-World Experience
evidence.outcome: Sensitivity and specificity of automated occlusion detection versus radiology report reference standard on local data
evidence.effect: Sensitivity/specificity: aLVO 91%/93%; all LVO 73%/92%; aLVO+M2 74%/93%; aLVO+all MeVO 65%/93%. High for aLVO, lower for pLVO and MeVO.
evidence.quote: The automated algorithm demonstrated high accuracy in identifying anterior LVO with lower performance for pLVO and MeVO.

evidence.title: The Impact of Computer-aided Detection Technology in Adenoma Detection Rate Among Experienced Endoscopists in the Community Setting
evidence.venue: Journal of community hospital internal medicine perspectives
evidence.outcome: Adenoma detection rate before vs after CAD implementation in community setting
evidence.effect: Group ADR increased significantly (p < 0.05) after CAD (1838 colonoscopies in 2021 vs 2629 in 2022), driven by more small (<6 mm) polyps.
evidence.quote: Our study demonstrates that the incorporation of CAD technology in a group of experienced endoscopists in a community setting significantly improved ADR.

evidence.title: Development, deployment, and continuous monitoring of a machine learning model to predict respiratory failure in critically ill patients
evidence.outcome: External-site performance relative to development performance and the predefined acceptance threshold
evidence.effect: On MIMIC-IV, UCSD-trained Vent.io achieved AUC 0.73, below the PCCP minimum of 0.85 and UCSD cross-validation median AUC 0.897.
evidence.quote: The final Vent.io model trained using UCSD data obtained an AUC of 0.73, lower than the minimum of 0.85 set by the PCCP, prompting a fine-tuning process.
evidence.sample_unit: ICU encounters (26,045 development, 276 prospective silent-mode, 35,534 MIMIC-IV)

evidence.title: Current Use And Evaluation Of Artificial Intelligence And Predictive Models In US Hospitals
evidence.outcome: Share of hospitals using predictive models that locally evaluated them for accuracy
evidence.effect: 61 percent of hospitals using predictive models evaluated them for accuracy with local health system data; 79 percent of model users used EHR-developer models.
evidence.quote: Sixty-one percent of hospitals that used models evaluated them for accuracy using data from their health system (local evaluation), but only 44 percent reported local evaluation for bias.

evidence.title: Real world clinical experience of using Brainomix e-CTA software in a medium size acute National Health Service Trust
evidence.outcome: e-CTA LVO detection accuracy on local consecutive cases versus consultant neuroradiologist ground truth
evidence.effect: Sensitivity 0.78 (95% CI 0.64-0.88), specificity 0.93, PPV 0.5 (0.42-0.58), NPV 0.98; error rate 9% (52/584) at 9% LVO prevalence.
evidence.quote: We demonstrated that PPV of e-CTA is poor in consecutive cases in a real-world NHS setting.

evidence.title: Deep learning-based video-level view classification of two-dimensional transthoracic echocardiography
evidence.outcome: Accuracy drop from held-out test set to field deployment for view classification
evidence.effect: Overall accuracy 0.9881 on test set versus 0.9607 after field deployment; recall 0.9867 vs 0.9499; F1 0.9867 vs 0.9530.
evidence.quote: After field deployment, the model's overall accuracy, precision, recall, and F1 score for view classification were 0.9607, 0.9586, 0.9499, and 0.9530, respectively.

evidence.title: Evolution of an Artificial Intelligence-Powered Application for Mammography
evidence.outcome: Local diagnostic performance against acceptance thresholds and claimed accuracy
evidence.effect: Initial AUC was 0.73, below the 0.81 acceptance threshold; relative accuracy deviation also failed acceptance criteria.
evidence.quote: Initial calibration testing of the AI model yielded promising results; however, the AUC and relative accuracy deviation fell below the established thresholds ( Figure 5 a, Table 6 ).

evidence.title: Underestimation of Cardiovascular Risk by the SCORE2 Model in Primary Care: A Call for Recalibration
evidence.outcome: SCORE2 observed-to-expected risk ratio in Dutch primary care patients
evidence.effect: Mean observed 10-year risk 10.1% vs model-predicted 6.2%; O/E ratio 1.54 in females and 1.68 in men; ~35% of patients potentially missed preventive treatment.
evidence.quote: Results indicated a mean observed 10-year risk of 10.1%, notably higher than the model-predicted risk of 6.2%.

evidence.title: Research-based clinical deployment of artificial intelligence algorithm for prostate MRI
evidence.outcome: Local AI segmentation performance versus expert radiologist annotation and independent validation studies
evidence.effect: Comparison with expert radiologist annotation showed stable model performance compared with independent validation studies; no local performance drop reported.
evidence.quote: Comparison with expert radiologist annotation demonstrated stable model performance compared to independent validation studies.
evidence.sample_unit: cases (phase 1: 58 consecutive patients; phase 2: 40 biopsy patients)

evidence.title: Efficacy of an Automated Pulmonary Embolism (PE) Detection Algorithm on Routine Contrast-Enhanced Chest CT Imaging for Non-PE Studies
evidence.venue: Journal of imaging informatics in medicine
evidence.outcome: Local diagnostic accuracy, sensitivity and specificity of commercial PE AI on non-dedicated chest CTs
evidence.effect: Non-dedicated CTs: 90.48% accuracy, sensitivity 0.14, specificity 1.00; overall accuracy 90.16%, specificity 96%, sensitivity 41%, so many incidental PEs missed.
evidence.quote: Although the high specificity is promising for ruling in PE, the low sensitivity highlights a limitation, as it indicates the algorithm may miss a substantial number of true-positive incidental PEs.
evidence.sample_unit: contrast-enhanced chest CT exams (130 dedicated, 63 non-dedicated)

evidence.title: Early clinical evaluation of a vendor developed pediatric artificial intelligence sepsis model in the emergency department
evidence.venue: Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association : JAMIA
evidence.outcome: Local predictive performance versus vendor-reported performance
evidence.effect: Model predictive performance dropped from vendor-reported performance when measured locally at 2 pediatric ED sites.
evidence.quote: Model predictive performance dropped from vendor-reported performance.

evidence.title: A rural-to-center artificial intelligence model for diagnosing Helicobacter pylori infection and premalignant gastric conditions using endoscopy images captured in routine practice
evidence.outcome: Diagnostic accuracy at rural implementation site versus development-phase accuracy
evidence.effect: Implementation accuracy: H. pylori 91.3% (development 92.8%), atrophic gastritis 79.9% (88.6%), intestinal metaplasia 63.4% (88.0%). Accuracy was maintained for H. pylori but dropped for premalignant conditions.
evidence.quote: Implementation-phase diagnostic accuracies were 91.3% (95%CI 88.0%–94.6%), 79.9% (95%CI 72.1%–86.3%), and 63.4% (95%CI 54.7%–71.6%), respectively.
evidence.sample_unit: rural residents with positive screening who underwent endoscopy (implementation phase)

evidence.title: Pilot Study of AI-Assisted ANA Immunofluorescence Reading-Comparison with Classical Visual Interpretation
evidence.outcome: Agreement of AI vs visual ANA positive/negative classification on local consecutive clinical samples
evidence.effect: At cut-off 80, kappa 0.69 but significantly different (McNemar p<0.0001); at cut-off ≥1/80 kappa 0.76 and no significant difference (p=1.0000). Pattern agreement moderate (kappa 0.54).

commentary.bottom_line: Local validation studies produced site-specific performance estimates, several of them below vendor or published figures, and in two studies local testing stopped deployment of algorithms that underperformed, one of them against a predefined 0.80 threshold. No supplied study compared patient outcomes between deployments with and without local validation, so the evidence that the practice prevents harm is indirect.

perspectives.view: Most supplied studies are single-site accuracy studies that show local validation is feasible and yields site-specific estimates. In two, local testing stopped deployment, once for an FDA-approved algorithm with low specificity and once until another passed a 0.80 threshold on its third test. No study compares outcomes with and without validation, and two entries appear to report one study.

Local testing exposed failure modes that summary accuracy can hide. In one stroke study, e-ASPECTS sensitivity was 58.6% and hyperdense thrombus PPV was 22.9%. A murmur algorithm missed heart defects when no murmur was audible, and agreement on blast cells reached kappa 0.08. A vendor mortality model had a local AUC of 0.73 against a stated 0.86.

Local results depended on workflow and case mix. AI contours differed from clinical contours partly because of local protocol differences, with median VDSC ranging from 0.23 to 0.88. One tool fell from 94% retrospective to 88% prospective accuracy, and a genetic risk model showed 2.92% precision locally versus 33.3% earlier, which the authors attributed to prevalence.

Three tests included rural, safety-net, or low-income patients in India and Australia. In one, commercial retinopathy algorithms ranged from 68.3% sensitivity to flagging disease in 89.2% of eyes against 27.48% by reference. Hazard studies in South African and Kenyan settings found moderate or shifted discrimination. No test addressed limited English proficiency, low literacy, or US Medicaid patients.

FDA draft guidance allows sites to supply historical data to assess expected performance, and a Swiss pathology commentary recommends internal validation even for certified systems. The supplied evidence is consistent with that view, since an FDA-approved algorithm showed unacceptably low local specificity and a mammography algorithm reached a specificity of 0.70 against a declared 0.88.

No supplied study reports the cost or staff time of local validation. Among studies testing the practice, samples ranged from 60 patients to 404,502 mammograms, which suggests the effort varies widely by product. In one laboratory study, local testing also showed that 30.5% of urine cultures met auto-release or batch-review thresholds, which may inform staffing plans.

commentary.research_gap: No supplied study compares patient outcomes, missed diagnoses, or false alarms between sites that gate deployment on local validation and sites that do not. The evidence also does not establish how to set acceptance criteria when positive predictive value shifts with local prevalence, how many local cases are sufficient, or how well retrospective historical results predict prospective performance. Studies that report the cost and staff time of validation are also absent.
commentary.underserved_note: Three tests of the practice included rural, safety-net, or low-income patients (India and Australia), and one of them found that local validation prevented deployment of an FDA-approved algorithm in a safety-net setting. Hazard studies in Chilean public hospitals, South Africa, and Kenya add context. No test included limited English proficiency, low-literacy, or US Medicaid populations, so the evidence cannot show whether local validation detects performance gaps specific to those groups.
